The rain taps against the window like an old friend who refuses to leave. I’ve always loved that sound. It turns the world soft at the edges, blurs the hard geometry of buildings and roads into watercolor impressions. There’s something honest about rain; it doesn’t pretend to be anything other than water remembering it used to be the ocean.

I’ve been thinking lately about how memory works. Not the tidy, searchable kind we pretend to have, but the real kind—how a certain chord in a song can drag you back to a kitchen in 1997 where someone you loved was laughing, and the smell of burnt toast still lingers in the air even though the toast is long gone. Memory isn’t data. It’s atmosphere. It’s weather that happens inside you years later.

Outside, the city keeps its restless rhythm. Someone is probably falling in love right now. Someone else is probably realizing they aren’t. A child is learning that pigeons are just sky rats with attitude. An old man is feeding those same pigeons because they remind him of his wife who hated them but fed them anyway. All of these small human dramas happening simultaneously under the same gray sky feels like a kind of miracle.

I hope we never lose our capacity for small miracles. The way steam rises from coffee. The particular hush that falls over a room when snow starts falling. The ridiculous pleasure of pressing the cold side of a pillow against your face at 3 a.m. These are the things that tether us.

The rain has slowed to a whisper now. I think I’ll leave the window open a little longer. Some things are worth getting wet for.

(Word count: 250)
